What strength reading glasses do I need?
answer_text: Quick rule of thumb based on age: 40-44 → +1.00, 45-49 → +1.25 to +1.50, 50-54 → +1.50 to +1.75, 55-59 → +2.00 to +2.25, 60+ → +2.50 to +3.00. For a more accurate reading use a printable diopter test chart at 14 inches. If between strengths, always pick the lower number. More details: https://teenyoun.github.io/eyewear-guide/articles/reading-glasses-strength-guide.html

question: Are expensive glasses worth it?
answer_text: I ordered prescription glasses at $6, $50, $150, and $400 and tested them with a lensometer. All four met ANSI accuracy standards. The sweet spot is $30-80 online — polycarbonate lenses with anti-reflective coating. Above $200 you're paying for brand name and premium materials. question: How to stop glasses from slipping down nose?
answer_text: Cheapest fix: adhesive silicone nose pads ($5 for 10 pairs). They prevent sliding on oily skin. Silicone ear hooks ($5) go on temple arms behind your ears — invisible when worn. For a permanent fix, an optician can adjust your temple bend for free in 30 seconds. 10 solutions here: https://teenyoun.github.io/eyewear-guide/articles/how-to-stop-glasses-from-slipping-down-your-nose-10-simple-fixes.html

question: Do the cheap sunglasses have good UV protection?
answer_text: A dark tint and UV protection are two different things, and it is entirely possible to buy sunglasses that are very dark and protect your eyes badly. The tint controls visible light; UV protection is a property of the lens material and its UV-absorbing treatment, so a deeply tinted lens with no UV treatment can suppress the light that makes you squint while passing ultraviolet through. Look for an explicit UV400 claim (blocks up to 400 nm, covering the UVA and UVB range that matters for the eye) rather than judging by darkness, and treat filter category 0-4 as a separate decision about visible light. My longer explainer: https://teenyoun.com/articles/what-uv400-actually-means-and-why-a-dark-tint-is-not-uv-protection.html

question: Are high index lenses worth it, or are they merely cosmetic?
answer_text:
Not cosmetic, but not automatically worth it either. The honest answer depends on your prescription power.

Index describes how strongly a material bends light, so for the same power a higher-index lens can be made thinner. That part is real optics, not marketing.

The cost is dispersion, and the Abbe number measures it. CR-39 sits near 1.50 with an Abbe number around 58; polycarbonate is about 1.586 with an Abbe number near 30; the 1.67 and 1.74 materials land in the low 30s as well. A lower Abbe number means more chromatic aberration, which shows up as colour fringing toward the edge of the lens and reduced contrast away from the optical centre. Higher-index surfaces also reflect more light, which is why these lenses benefit so much from a good anti-reflective coating.

Two things people usually miss. First, higher-index materials are generally denser, so a thinner lens is not automatically a lighter one. Second, the thickness you actually save scales with your prescription: at a mild power the millimetres saved are small enough that the better optical quality of a lower-index material may serve you better, while at a strong minus power the saving is the difference between a comfortable lens and a heavy one. In practice, many opticians start steering people toward higher index from roughly plus or minus 3 dioptres and up.

I wrote a longer breakdown of index, Abbe number and dispersion here: https://teenyoun.com/articles/lens-index-and-abbe-number-why-thinner-glasses-aren-t-always-better.html
